system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2153-04-20 18:20:00 to 2153-04-21 17:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with right-sided abdominal and flank pain described as a burning sensation, initially of unknown cause. Imaging ruled out acute abdominal pathology, diverticulitis, or obstruction. A vesicular rash developed along the right T5/6 dermatome, leading to a diagnosis of localized varicella zoster (shingles) by dermatology, despite a negative viral swab. She was treated with IV acyclovir, later transitioned to oral valacyclovir, with clinical improvement. Liver enzymes were elevated, attributed to possible hepatic zoster or GVHD, prompting an increase in prednisone from 15mg to 20mg daily and initiation of Bactrim for PCP prophylaxis. Epigastric pain emerged late in the admission, managed with Maalox and ranitidine after normal amylase, lipase, and imaging. The patient stabilized, pain improved with pregabalin, and she was discharged home on updated medications with follow-up planned.
problems: Herpes zoster without mention of complication
Peripheral stem cells replaced by transplant
Nonspecific elevation of levels of transaminase or lactic acid dehydrogenase [LDH]

demonstrated.  Both are non-compressibile with no discernible color flow, and
a subtle venous waveform, all compatible with non-occlusive thrombus.  The
remaining veins demonstrate normal compressibility, flow, and augmentation.

IMPRESSION:  Non-occlusive DVT of the left posterior tibial veins; this
finding was communicated to ___ at 17:04 on ___ by ___
___ over the phone.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with left lower extremity DVT, worsening
dyspnea.

COMPARISON:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT data were acquired before and after the administration of
intravenous contrast.  Images were displayed in multiple planes including
oblique projections.

FINDINGS:  Contrast bolus timing is suboptimal for evaluation of the pulmonary
arteries as the images were acquired in an arterial phase.  Despite these
limitations, a filling defect is clearly noted at the junction of the right
middle and lower lobe pulmonary arteries (3:46, 402B:35).  Thrombus extends
down the right lower lobe pulmonary artery (3:48) and fills several right
basilar branches (3:52).  Thrombus also appears in the right upper lobe
pulmonary artery (3:35).  The left main and segmental pulmonary arteries are
patent.  Poor bolus timing limits detection of subsegmental emboli.  An
equivocal filling defect is seen in the anterior basal left pulmonary artery
(3:61).

No new nodules, consolidations, or effusions are seen in the lungs.  A 4-mm
right upper lobe granuloma is unchanged (2:21).  Calcified nodes are seen at
the left hilus (2:35).  The airways are patent to the subsegmental level.  No
pathologic mediastinal, hilar, or axillary adenopathy is present.  Coronary
artery calcifications are seen in the proximal LAD (2:25).  Thyroid gland
enhances homogeneously.  The visualized portions of the upper abdomen
demonstrate homogenously enhancing portions of the liver.  A tiny splenic
granuloma is noted.  The adrenal glands are normal.  Upper poles of both
kidneys enhance and excrete contrast symmetrically.  Surgical clips are seen
in the cholecystectomy bed and one clip is posterior to the right lobe of the
liver (3:10).  An 8-mm coarse calcification in the medial right breast is
unchanged since ___.

IMPRESSION:  Acute pulmonary emboli to the right upper, middle, and lower
pulmonary arteries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. You came in today because of pain in your left calf?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been hurting more since I got back from visiting my mom. It feels tight and really aches when I walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned some shortness of breath and chest discomfort at night, especially when lying down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been worse lately. I get a bit of cough and wheezing at night. But no chest pain during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of a prior blood clot and recent travel, we’re concerned about a possible clot in your leg or lungs. We’ve done an ultrasound on your legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Did they find anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the ultrasound showed a blood clot in the deep veins of your left calf. That explains the pain and swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds serious. Could it have traveled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we ordered a CT scan of your chest. Because of your breathing symptoms, we needed to check for a pulmonary embolism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. I’m sorry to say it shows blood clots in the arteries of your right lung. That’s what’s causing your shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no… is it dangerous? Are my lungs okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable right now. No strain on your heart, and your oxygen levels are good. We’re starting you on a blood thinner called Lovenox to prevent more clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to be on that forever? I’ve had a clot before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of a prior PE and now this new one, it’s likely you’ll need long-term anticoagulation. We’ll discuss that with your oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look better today. Your breathing has improved, and you walked the hallway without any drop in oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I do feel less short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discharge you today with Lovenox injections twice a day. You’ll also keep taking your other medications, including prednisone for your GVHD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eye drops? I haven’t been using them regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please restart Systane every hour and Restasis twice a day. Your dry eyes are part of your chronic GVHD and need consistent care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try to be better about that. And my headaches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can continue oxycodone as needed, up to every 8 hours. But let your doctor know if they worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I follow up with my oncologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. They’ll manage your long-term anticoagulation and GVHD. We’ve sent them all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have the discharge papers ready soon. Keep using your medications as prescribed and call if you have chest pain or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, really. My leg feels better, and I can breathe normally now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Remember to inject Lovenox every 12 hours and follow up with your team. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with worsening left calf pain and nighttime respiratory symptoms following recent travel. Imaging confirmed a deep vein thrombosis in the left posterior tibial veins, and a CT angiogram revealed acute pulmonary emboli in the right upper, middle, and lower pulmonary arteries. She remained hemodynamically stable without need for thrombolysis. Anticoagulation with Lovenox was initiated, leading to clinical improvement in respiratory symptoms and ambulatory tolerance. Chronic issues including graft-versus-host disease affecting the eyes, skin, and mouth were managed with ongoing prednisone and eye medications. The patient was discharged home on Lovenox with plans for long-term anticoagulation and follow-up with her oncologist.
